Cybersecurity firm Palo Alto Networks raised its annual revenue forecast and agreed to acquire AI startup Applied Compute for $4.5 billion. Shares of Palo Alto Networks jumped about 9% in after-hours trading on Wednesday to $368.70, driving gains among its rivals.
Palo Alto Networks has been positioning itself as an integrated cybersecurity provider through a series of recent acquisitions. With the acquisition of Applied Compute, the company aims to offer a technology platform that helps customers securely train and deploy open-weight AI models as they expand their use of artificial intelligence.
Palo Alto Networks said it believes the future of enterprise AI will be hybrid, with a large share of enterprises running open-source and open-weight models tailored to their data, cost and control requirements.
Read: IIT Kharagpur alumni’s Unsiloed AI raises $7.5 million to make business documents AI-ready (November 18, 2026)
The acquisition will enable Palo Alto Networks to help enterprises train, adapt and deploy open-weight AI models with security built in, whether in public cloud environments or sovereign infrastructure. According to the company, this will help organizations strengthen compliance and security. Applied Compute will continue serving AI-native companies, digital-native businesses and large enterprises, while Palo Alto Networks will bring its platform to its global customer base.
Palo Alto Networks said Applied Compute has one of the industry’s strongest AI research teams. Its team will join Palo Alto Networks, with Applied Compute co-founder and CEO Yash Patil set to become Palo Alto Networks’ co-chief AI officer following the close of the transaction .
“Applied Compute extends Palo Alto’s push beyond traditional cybersecurity into enterprise AI,” TD Cowen analyst Shaul Eyal said.
The deal is expected to close in the third quarter of fiscal 2027.
Read: Sahir Raoof launches $27.5 million VC fund betting on AI to reshape pharma services (November 11, 2026)
Palo Alto Networks now expects fiscal 2027 revenue to reach between $14.52 billion and $14.57 billion, compared with its previous forecast of $14.10 billion to $14.20 billion.
The company’s first-quarter revenue reached $3.45 billion, up 39% from a year earlier and above analysts’ estimates of $3.31 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG.
Palo Alto Networks is also in talks to acquire Clutch Security for $500 million in cash, along with additional milestone-based payments, according to a person familiar with the matter.
Clutch is a three-year-old startup that was last valued at $85 million when it raised a $20 million Series A funding round in January 2025, led by Lightspeed and SignalFire.
The company is currently approaching $10 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR). If completed, the acquisition would value Clutch at approximately 50 times its ARR, a common metric used to value software companies.

State utility CFE successfully raised US$776 million through a CFE Fibra E follow-on equity offering, attracting strong investor demand. This capital will fund critical transmission projects, modernize national grid infrastructure, and alleviate severe power bottlenecks to support nearshoring and industrial growth across Mexico through 2030.
The state utility CFE has successfully raised US$776 million through a follow-on equity offering executed via its transmission investment vehicle, CFE Fibra E. This financial milestone marks a significant return to public equity markets for the utility since its initial public listing in 2018. The transaction experienced exceptionally robust investor appetite, drawing a total of US$1.64 billion in demand, which represents 3.2 times the size of the base offering. Notably, the World Bank's International Finance Corporation (IFC) participated actively in the transaction as an anchor investor. Capital generated from this successful equity offering will directly fund essential transmission projects nationwide, reinforcing national grid infrastructure, connecting new generation assets, and alleviating critical energy bottlenecks across strategic industrial corridors.
The successful execution of CFE Fibra E's follow-on offering highlights a crucial strategic shift in how Mexico finances large-scale electrical infrastructure. By leveraging innovative public-private investment vehicles and attracting institutional participation from multilateral bodies like the IFC, the state utility is channeling private capital directly into grid modernization without relying solely on restrictive annual public budgets. As analyzed in [Infrastructure 2027 Can Mexico Move Its Growth]([link removed]), establishing predictable funding mechanisms and expanding transmission capacity are vital for preventing operational friction across high-freight and industrial manufacturing clusters. The earmarked funds will specifically target critical bottlenecks across prioritized transmission projects, expanding substation capacity, reinforcing high-voltage lines, and building the necessary physical backbone to stabilize regional power supplies and accommodate rising commercial loads through 2030.
While nearshoring has superintended unprecedented demand for industrial real estate, warehouses, and advanced manufacturing facilities across northern border hubs and central manufacturing zones, electrical distribution constraints have increasingly threatened to slow investment momentum. Industrial park developers and corporate tenants frequently encounter prolonged delays for high-voltage grid connections, which can stretch past two years in high-demand submarkets. As detailed in [Mexico's Industrial Real Estate Boom Faces Infrastructure Gaps]([link removed]), trade uncertainty, electricity distribution bottlenecks, and resource availability are forming complex obstacles that require immediate infrastructural remedies. By directing fresh capital into transmission assets, CFE's latest capital raise addresses the core vulnerability holding back industrial park ramp-ups, ensuring that incoming manufacturing operations, logistics centers, and export facilities have reliable access to high-voltage power.
The rapid expansion of specialized industrial assets—including data centers, automated logistics hubs, and advanced automotive manufacturing plants—demands unprecedented levels of electrical reliability, continuous cooling, and robust grid connectivity. Constructing these specialized facilities requires navigating complex engineering hurdles, where access to dependable power is just as critical as the construction schedule itself. As discussed in [How Construction Will Define Infrastructure Behind Our Future]([link removed]), electricity availability remains a primary obstacle for industry specialists, with 56% of surveyed professionals identifying power access as a major challenge and nearly a third reporting that grid connections take more than two years. Integrating upgraded substations and transmission lines supported by Fibra E proceeds will directly mitigate these operational risks, providing the foundational reliability required for continuous commercial activities in key markets like Monterrey and Querétaro.
For B2B executives, energy developers, and industrial real estate investors operating in Mexico, the successful capitalization of CFE Fibra E represents an encouraging step toward resolving chronic grid congestion and unlocking stranded renewable energy generation. As federal authorities and state utilities advance infrastructure initiatives through 2030, aligning commercial expansion with accelerated transmission investments will determine the long-term competitiveness of Mexico's industrial landscape. Telangana Tech 9M 2026 Report: CtrlS, Skyroot Drive $726M Funding Surge as Seed Deals Decline
Spotlight Posted on November 20, 2026 • Updated November 20, 2026 —by Salil Urunkar
Share
Share on WhatsApp
Share on X
Share on LinkedIn
Share on Telegram
Hyderabad: Telangana’s technology funding market recorded a sharp increase in capital inflows during the first nine months of 2026, but the growth was concentrated in a small number of large transactions.
Companies across the state raised $726 million between January and September, a 266% jump from $199 million in the same period last year, even as the number of funding rounds declined 30%.
Join our WhatsApp community Subscribe to our email newsletter
The Telangana Tech 9M 2026 Report, released by Tracxn Technologies on November 20, shows that a single $423 million investment in Hyderabad-based data centre operator CtrlS accounted for 58% of the total funding raised during the period.
The transaction also contributed approximately 80% of the year-on-year increase in funding.
The contrast between rising investment value and falling deal activity points to an increasingly concentrated funding environment, with large enterprise infrastructure transactions driving the headline numbers while seed-stage investments and investor participation contracted.
Telangana recorded 73 funding rounds in 9M 2026, compared with 105 in the corresponding period of 2025. The average round size consequently climbed to $9.9 million from $1.9 million.
CtrlS, Skyroot Aerospace Lead Telangana’s Biggest Funding Deals
CtrlS dominated the funding landscape with two transactions during the period. The Hyderabad-based data centre company raised $28.2 million in a Series A round in February, followed by a $423 million Series B round in June, backed by CPP Investments.
Its combined fundraising during the nine months reached $451 million.
The scale of the transaction is reflected in the concentration of capital across the ecosystem. Telangana’s ten largest funding rounds collectively raised $664 million, accounting for 91% of the state’s total funding.
Space technology company Skyroot Aerospace secured $60 million in a Series C round in May, while Edubuk raised $50 million through a Series B round in March.
Beyond these large transactions, the funding pipeline showed signs of moderation. Series A and later-stage rounds declined 18% to 23, while the number of companies receiving funding for the first time dropped 31% to 20.
Early-Stage Funding Rises, but Seed Investments Decline
Early-stage funding emerged as the largest investment category, attracting $622 million during 9M 2026, compared with $143 million a year earlier. The segment accounted for 86% of Telangana’s total funding.
However, the increase was largely influenced by the CtrlS Series B transaction, which alone represented 68% of early-stage funding. The number of early-stage rounds declined 27% to 19.
Seed-stage activity also weakened, with funding falling 35% to $26.4 million from $40.6 million in 9M 2025. The number of seed rounds dropped from 77 to 50, indicating a slowdown in capital reaching companies at the earliest stages of development.
Late-stage funding, meanwhile, increased to $78.1 million from $14.8 million, across four rounds compared with two in the previous year. Despite the 426% increase, the segment remained significantly below the $482 million recorded in 9M 2024.
Enterprise Infrastructure Drives Telangana’s Funding Growth
The concentration of investment was particularly evident in the sectoral distribution of funding.
Enterprise Infrastructure companies attracted $454 million, accounting for approximately 63% of all funding raised in Telangana. The segment had raised just $13 million in the corresponding period of 2025.
Enterprise Applications ranked second with $142 million, an increase of 79% from $79.4 million. Aerospace, Maritime and Defense Tech also gained traction, attracting $78.5 million compared with $14.4 million a year earlier.
The sectoral numbers underline the growing importance of capital-intensive technology businesses, particularly infrastructure and aerospace companies, in Telangana’s funding landscape.
Hyderabad accounted for the entirety of the state’s technology funding during 9M 2026, compared with 98% in the year-ago period. This further strengthened the city’s dominance within Telangana’s technology ecosystem.
Telangana Tech 9M 2026 Report: Investor Participation Falls Despite Higher Funding
The rise in funding value was not accompanied by an increase in the number of investors participating in the ecosystem.
Tracxn recorded 61 active investors during the period, down 22% from 78 in 9M 2025. International investor participation declined 43% to 13, while the number of first-time investors fell 36% to 30.
Among the investors active in the state, Aum Ventures and V3 Ventures made two seed-stage investments each. Prosus led early-stage investment activity with investments in Equal and Deccan AI.
The decline in both international and first-time investor participation suggests that the funding increase was not necessarily indicative of a wider expansion in the investor base.
Skyroot Aerospace Becomes Telangana’s Only New Unicorn
On the startup milestone front, Skyroot Aerospace became Telangana’s only new unicorn during the first nine months of 2026. The Hyderabad-based space technology company, which develops launch vehicles for small satellites, achieved a valuation of at least $1 billion in May.
The state added no new unicorns during the corresponding period of 2025. However, the number of soonicorns, or companies tracked by Tracxn as potential future unicorns, declined 67% to four from 12.

Science’s $400M Series D Tops Week’s 10 Biggest Rounds
Dr. Heinrich Vogel
Updated Nov 21, 2026 · 14 min read
Photo: Amel Uzunovic / Pexels
Neurotech took the top slot in this week’s tally of the biggest funding rounds. Science, the brain-computer interface company based in Alameda, California, secured $400 million in Series D funding , according to reports from Crunchbase News, Traders Union, Techloy, ET Enterprise AI and EU-Startups. The round leads a list of ten large deals that also spans AI, fintech and biotech.

Why does this article cover only four of the ten rounds?
Three more rounds are confirmed in detail. Model ML closed a $250 million Series B, Galvanize Therapeutics raised $130 million in Series D funding, and Marrow Therapeutics launched with $173 million across Series A and Series B. Those four deals add up to $953 million. The remaining six rounds could not be verified from the available reporting, so this article does not list them. The lopsided shape of the week matches what we saw in NYC Series A deals falling to 44 from 82 in Q3 , where capital kept flowing to fewer, larger companies.
This piece sorts what is confirmed from what is not, compares the four deals, and explains why they matter for readers who follow AI and venture funding. It files under the AI and machine learning coverage on this site because two of the four headline companies sell AI-driven products and the other two sit at the edge of the same investor appetite for deep technology.

What this week’s biggest funding rounds tell us
A weekly funding list is a snapshot, and snapshots mislead when read alone. Still, this one carries a clear signal. The largest check went to a company building hardware that talks to the brain. The second largest went to a software platform for banks and professional services firms. The third and fourth went to medical technology and drug development. None of those four is a consumer app, and none depends on advertising revenue.
That mix says something about where investors are placing size bets in late 2026. They are favoring companies with long development cycles, regulated customers and products that are hard to copy. A brain-computer interface needs clinical evidence. A financial AI platform needs trust from compliance teams. An ablation device needs regulators. A marrow-targeted therapy needs trials. Each of those barriers protects margins if the company clears them.

The story is also a reminder to read headlines with care. The title of the week’s roundup promises ten deals, but reporting available to us confirms only four. We treat the other six as unconfirmed and say so in a later section.
Science’s $400 million Series D, in detail
Science secured $400 million in Series D funding for brain-computer interface and neural-engineering technology. Reports put the company’s total funding above $900 million. The company was founded in 2021 and is headquartered in Alameda, California.
The arithmetic is worth a pause. If total funding sits just above $900 million, this single round accounts for roughly 44 percent of everything Science has raised, or a little less. That means the company has pulled in close to half its lifetime capital in one financing, five years after it was founded. Few private companies in any sector can claim that, and fewer still in a field where no product has yet reached mass adoption.
What PRIMA is
Reports identify PRIMA as Science’s vision-restoration brain-computer-interface device. That is the extent of what the verified information supports. We do not have clinical results, approval status, patient counts or launch timing for PRIMA from the sources available to us, so we do not state any. Readers who want those details should check the company’s own announcements and the original outlets.
The valuation question
Some secondary reporting mentions a $3.5 billion valuation for Science. We could not confirm that figure from primary information, so treat it as unverified. A valuation attached to a round is not the same as a number the company has disclosed, and a mid-sized private deal can be reported at several different figures depending on how preferred shares and options are counted.

Want to keep track of the largest startup funding deals in 2026 with our curated list of $100 million-plus venture deals to U.S.-based companies? Check out The Crunchbase Megadeals Board .
This is a weekly feature that runs down the week’s Top 10 announced funding rounds in the U.S. Check out last week’s biggest funding deal roundup here .
It was a big week for tech startup exits, headlined by Anthropic pulling off its massive IPO. On the down side, however, tech stocks took a huge dive in the past few days. Should that negative sentiment and downward pressure persist, we can expect it to spill over into private markets.
For this past week, however, U.S. startups continued to secure sizable rounds, led by brain-computer interface company Science landing a fresh $400 million. Another seven American companies announced venture or growth funding of $100 million or more, and across the Atlantic, UK-based AI biotech startup Isomorphic Labs landed $5 billion, the largest financing of the week.
1. Science , $400M, neurotech : Science, a startup focused on brain-computer interface technology, and neural engineering, secured $400 million in Series D funding. The round brings total funding to date for the Alameda, California-based company to more than $900 million.
2. Model ML , $250M, AI and fintech : Model ML, an AI platform for financial and professional services, closed on $250 million in Series B funding at a $1.5 billion valuation. General Atlantic and QED Investors led the round for the three-year-old company, which is based in New York and London.
3. Galvanize Therapeutics , $130M, biotech : Redwood City, California-based Galvanize Therapeutics, a developer of pulsed electric field ablation technologies for oncology and chronic disease, picked up $130 million in Series D funding led by HealthQuest Capital .
4. General Flash , $128M, critical metals : General Flash, a developer of a new method to produce critical metals, announced that it has raised $128 million across seed and Series A rounds from a long list of investors.
5. Ramon.Space , $124M, space tech : Denver-based Ramon.Space, a developer of space computing infrastructure, pulled in $124M in Series B funding led by PSG .
6. Marrow Therapeutics , $120M, biotech : Watertown, Massachusetts-based Marrow Therapeutics, a developer of bone marrow-targeted therapies to treat severe blood disorders, announced its launch with a combined $173 million in Series A and B funding. Orbimed led its $120 million Series B round while Scion Life Sciences and venBio led the $53 million Series A.
7. Noeri , $110M, enterprise AI : Noeri, a developer of self-improving AI for enterprises and researchers, launched with $110 million in initial funding. Menlo Ventures led the round for the Palo Alto-based startup, which was founded by Stanford University computer science professors.
8. Seawolf Therapeutics , $100M, biotech : San Diego-based Seawolf Therapeutics, a biotech startup developing a novel DNA delivery platform, emerged from stealth and announced that it has raised $100 million in funding to date, with Versant Ventures , MPM BioImpact and Novartis Venture Fund as lead investors.
9. BrightAI , $97M, physical AI : BrightAI, a startup developing a sensor, drone and robotics-driven platform to bring continuous observability to infrastructure-heavy industries like power, water, and energy, secured $97 million in new funding. Smith Point Capital led the financing for the Silicon Valley-based company.
10. Vincue , $93M, vehicle intelligence platform : Kansas City-based Vincue, developer of a vehicle lifecycle intelligence platform, closed on $93 million in growth capital led by Wavecrest Growth Partners .
And overseas:
Isomorphic Labs , $5B, AI and biotech : London-based Isomorphic Labs, a startup that applies AI to drug discovery, secured $5 billion in Series C funding. Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital led the financing for the five-year-old company, which also has offices in Massachusetts and Switzerland.
Methodology
We tracked the largest announced rounds in the Crunchbase database that were raised by U.S.-based companies for the period of Nov. 14-20, 2026. Although most announced rounds are in the database, there may be a small time lag, as some rounds are reported late in the week.

candidates.title: Marrow Therapeutics Launches With $173M Series A and B for Bone Marrow-Targeted Genetic Medicines
candidates.snippet: Marrow Therapeutics Launches With $173M Series A and B for Bone Marrow-Targeted Genetic Medicines Wowtale
candidates.text:
Marrow Therapeutics, a U.S. biotech startup built around antibodies that carry drugs only to bone marrow, has launched with $173 million in combined funding, a $53 million Series A and a $120 million Series B. It wants to treat sickle cell disease and beta thalassemia with a single injection.
Marrow Therapeutics is a genetic medicines company based in Watertown, Massachusetts. According to press reports, Scion Life Sciences formed and incubated it in 2024, and it spent nearly three years developing its technology quietly. It builds a drug delivery system that sends genetic medicines to a chosen place in the body and uses it to develop its own drugs, rather than only licensing the technology to others.
Sickle cell disease and beta thalassemia are inherited disorders of hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. In sickle cell disease, red cells bend into a sickle shape and block blood vessels; in beta thalassemia, the body cannot make enough healthy red cells. Patients live with lifelong anemia, pain and organ damage. Gene-editing therapies are already approved, but they are burdensome: a patient’s bone marrow stem cells are removed, their DNA is edited outside the body, and the cells are infused back after harsh chemotherapy that clears the marrow, at a list price of $2.2 million to $3.1 million (press reports).
Marrow goes after the same diseases differently. Before birth, babies carry oxygen with fetal hemoglobin, and after birth a gene called BCL11A switches it off. Turning that switch back down revives fetal hemoglobin and eases symptoms. Casgevy, the approved therapy, targets the same switch but edits cells outside the body. Marrow wants to turn it down with an injection that reaches the marrow directly, without removing any cells.
The platform is called TAB, short for Transferrin Antibody Bioconjugate. The antibody, a protein that sticks only to a specific target, is the delivery truck. Its destination is the transferrin receptor (TfR1), the door cells use to take in iron, which is especially abundant on the bone marrow cells that make blood. The cargo is siRNA, a small RNA molecule that stops a specific gene from being turned into protein. It does not change DNA; it removes the working copy of the gene’s instructions and turns its output down.
The first candidate, MAR-101, is the first drug built on the TAB platform: an antibody conjugated to an siRNA. It targets both diseases. According to press reports, the antibody carries an siRNA against BCL11A to bring back fetal hemoglobin production. It is in IND-enabling studies, the preclinical work needed before regulators allow tests in people, and press reports say the aim is a subcutaneous self-injection that is stable at room temperature. The company says monkey studies showed bone marrow target engagement, BCL11A knockdown and fetal hemoglobin induction, and that results in human cells are on par with or better than ex vivo editing approaches. It has not released the data, and MAR-101 has not been tested in people.
Using a receptor like TfR1 as the destination for drug delivery has been validated elsewhere. According to press reports, a drug from Denali that binds TfR was approved for Hunter syndrome in March, and Dyne Therapeutics and Avidity Biosciences use the same receptor for muscle diseases.
Questions remain, though. One outlet noted that Marrow raised its money without releasing anemia or selectivity data. Because TfR1 is how cells take in iron, an antibody that interferes with it could starve developing red blood cells of iron and cause anemia. The company says its experience with TfR1 lets it avoid that risk. TfR1 is also present on many cell types, and BCL11A is needed for B-cell development, so the question is whether the drug can be confined to the red-cell lineage. Because siRNA does not change DNA, how long the effect lasts and how often patients would need injections are also open. The company has not disclosed its antibody sequences or patent position.
Romesh Subramanian is President and CEO. According to press reports he was CEO and chief scientific officer of Dyne Therapeutics and later led Ascidian Therapeutics. Tim Weeden, chief scientific officer, has experience in transferrin receptor biology and antibody and nucleic acid development, and John Najim, chief operating officer and chief technology officer, leads chemistry, manufacturing and controls (CMC). Press reports say both also come from Dyne. Gavriel Mullokandov is founder and VP of corporate development. Art Levin, founding chief scientific officer of Avidity Biosciences, joined the board, and Stuart Orkin of Harvard Medical School joined the scientific advisory board.
Marrow announced the funding. Scion Life Sciences and venBio co-led the Series A, which press reports say was raised in early 2025 but not announced while Marrow shored up its intellectual property. OrbiMed led the Series B, with all Series A investors plus RTW Investments, Surveyor Capital (a Citadel company), Opaleye, NEXTBio Capital, Affinity Advisors, KKR , Spruce Street Capital and Columbia Threadneedle Investments. The company did not disclose a valuation.
According to press reports the money goes toward readying the clinic and building manufacturing capacity. It did not give a clinical start date, and Scion said it expects the programs to enter the clinic in the coming year.
Its competitors are the gene-editing therapies already on the market. According to press reports, Vertex ‘s Casgevy, which uses CRISPR to lower BCL11A expression, is approved at a $2.2 million list price, and Genetix ‘s Lyfgenia is priced at $3.1 million. Both require chemotherapy conditioning to clear the marrow. Efforts to edit stem cells inside the body continue as well: Tessera reported in May that it achieved average long-term blood stem cell editing of 85% in non-human primates, according to press reports.

Dreamteam, an AI-native customer relationship management (CRM) startup founded by former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million to take on established players such as Salesforce and HubSpot.

The funding came across two rounds, a seed round led by Together Fund and a Series A led by Accel , with Premji Invest also participating, according to TechCrunch . The startup did not disclose how much each round raised or its current valuation.
Dreamteam plans to use the funding to extend its platform beyond sales into other stages of the customer lifecycle, including prospecting, onboarding, customer success and upselling.
Who is behind Dreamteam
Founded in 2025 by Anand Venkatraman, Ramesh Parthasarathy and Senthil Kanthaswamy, the startup was established by three former senior executives at SaaS firm Freshworks who played key roles in its growth from an early-stage startup to a publicly listed company.
Venkatraman, who is the CEO, has spent more than 25 years in enterprise software, including at Salesforce and Freshworks. Kanthaswamy spent more than nine years at Freshworks and most recently led product at Freshservice, while Parthasarathy worked on AI and platform engineering at the startup.
Dreamteam is based in San Francisco and has more than 35 employees. Its engineering team sits in Chennai, while its go-to-market operations are run from the US.
Together Fund, co-founded by Freshworks co-founder Girish Mathrubootham, was the first institutional investor in Dreamteam.
How the product works
Traditional CRM software depends on sales teams typing in customer information and updating records by hand. Dreamteam is trying to remove most of that work.
Its platform is built around a system it calls Company Brain, which pulls information from emails, calendars, meetings, customer conversations and connected tools, and keeps a shared record of every customer relationship and business activity.
Four AI agents work on top of that record. Rachel researches leads and accounts, Sally drafts follow-up emails and suggests deal updates, Raj monitors the sales pipeline for risks, and Alex handles CRM setup and administration through conversational commands in plain English. The agents can also prepare meeting briefs and track commitments.
The startup said the agents only propose actions. Sales teams approve record updates and any communication that goes out to customers.
“ The CRM was supposed to give companies a complete picture of their customers, yet the richest parts of that picture have always lived outside the CRM, ” Venkatraman said.
“ AI finally gives us a way to change that foundation. Dreamteam learns from the work your team is already doing, keeps the context alive, and gives every salesperson skilled AI teammates that can reason over it and move deals forward, ” he added.
Dreamteam also offers Magic Apps, which lets users build applications and dashboards using natural language without writing code. For teams that want to work outside the usual CRM interface, it provides an API and an MCP server, and supports integrations with AI tools such as Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini .
Pricing and customers
Dreamteam's pricing page lists a single plan at $49 per seat per month, plus AI credit packs at $30 a month shared across the team. One pack covers 100 new contact enrichments and work on 20 live deals a month.
Venkatraman told TechCrunch that Dreamteam has signed up more than 100 customers across 13 countries in the three months since it began actively selling, and that most of them are paying. Kanthaswamy declined to disclose revenue. The startup is aiming for eight-figure annual revenue by the end of 2027.
Its customers come from sectors such as AI, online media, healthcare, manufacturing and consulting, and include DMS Health, InVideo and Plex.
Dreamteam said it replaced Salesforce at DMS Health and HubSpot at other customers, and that Plex's advertising sales team chose it over HubSpot and other AI-native CRM products. Some customers have expanded their initial pilots to their full sales teams, the company said.
What the investors said
“ AI is an equally massive opportunity, but it demands software rebuilt from the ground up, not AI layered onto legacy systems. CRM is among the biggest software categories ripe for disruption, ” Mathrubootham said.
Shekhar Kirani, partner at Accel, said Dreamteam was building a shared record of customer conversations and interactions that could give sales teams a common understanding of their customers.
Saravanan Nattanmai, partner at Premji Invest, said CRM systems needed to evolve from systems of record into systems of intelligence and action.
The global CRM market was valued at $79.6 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $161.3 billion by 2033, growing at about 9.3% a year, according to Grand View Research .
North America accounted for 40.4% of that revenue in 2025, while Asia Pacific is expected to grow the fastest. The research firm lists Salesforce, Microsoft, SAP, Oracle, Adobe, Zoho and Freshworks among the major companies in the market.

Today at 3:46 PM
Wingspire Commits $30 Million For Industrial Equipment Financing
Wingspire Equipment Finance has committed $30 million to finance equipment for an unidentified sponsor-backed industrial services company.
The facility is structured as an equipment line supporting material-handling equipment, transport assets, dump trucks, and related machinery.
Supporting New Contract Bids
The financing gives the company committed capital it can reference when bidding for customer contracts requiring additional equipment.
Wingspire is also providing progress funding as equipment is procured and prepared for deployment.

Wingspire designed the financing to address complexities arising from the company’s original carve-out acquisition and its continuing operating requirements.
Wingspire Equipment Finance provides equipment-financing solutions to middle-market and private equity-backed companies. It is part of Wingspire Capital, a portfolio company of Blue Owl Capital Corporation.

For our client, winning new business requires confidence that equipment capital will be available to take on new contracts. We structured a committed line with progress funding to help them secure the necessary assets and fulfill their customer commitments.

candidates.title: How to prepare your startup for a Series A raise in 2026
candidates.snippet: How to prepare your startup for a Series A raise in 2026 Techli
candidates.text:
For many startup founders, reaching the Series A stage is one of the most demanding transitions in building a company. The early excitement of launching a product, securing the first customers and celebrating initial revenue gradually gives way to a different set of responsibilities: proving to investors that the company is moving from experimental and early-stage products to a sustainable business that can generate revenue on repeatable basis.
Fewer and fewer founders are clearing that bar. Only 24% of U.S. startups that raised a seed round of $1 million USD or more in 2023 have since raised further funding, for example, according to Crunchbase data, down from a typical rate of 55% or higher for companies that raised seed rounds through 2020.
This is particularly relevant in 2026. U.S. startups raised approximately $42 billion in Series A funding through October, representing a 60% increase year over year, per Crunchbase. Yet, the number of deals has stayed roughly flat, meaning investors are writing bigger checks to a small group of companies that show the strongest potential for growth.
Revenue growth must be repeatable
While a strong revenue figure can help get a meeting with investors, it is not enough to secure funding. Some investors are writing larger checks at the seed stage, while others wait for later rounds of funding when there is more evidence of traction.
Here, founders must be able to prove that their early customers can be converted into a sustainable source of revenue for the company.
For Series A, investors are looking to understand how the company acquires customers, how long it takes to close a deal, and if growth can continue to scale with acquisition costs that are less than or equal to revenue growth, according to venture firm CRV. This means founders should prepare to discuss customer acquisition costs, gross margins, sales cycles, and cash burn for the company, in addition to revenue.
Retention is also critical. Whether the product solves a long-term problem for the customer and if the customer continues to use the product on a regular basis are key indicators of a startup’s success. Cohort analysis of customers, churn rates and net revenue retention (NRR) are key metrics that indicate whether there is sustainable demand for a startup’s product.
Carta’s Series A guidance , for example, outlines the key measures of product-market fit, revenue traction, healthy unit economics and a financial roadmap that are required for Series A funding.
Make the financial plan withstand scrutiny
A Series A financial model should connect the founders’ projections to operating evidence. Hiring plans, sales capacity, conversion rates, pricing, infrastructure costs and sales cycles can all support the founders’ forecast. Founders should explain their assumptions and prepare both a base-case and a downside scenario.
A big part of the Series A pitch is explaining what the funding will be used for; whether that is to hit a certain revenue number, enter a new market, or expand sales, the funding must be used to help the company reach measurable goals.
As the founder, you need to pull together your financial statements, current cap table, customer and revenue data, retention metrics, current contracts, and product metrics before going to market for Series A.
In sum, be ready to explain your customer concentration, churn, and delayed deals, as well as your growth.
Location is part of the growth strategy
The decision of where to incorporate is treated as an administrative decision, though it can certainly affect access to customers, talent, investment and predictable regulation in foreign markets.
Ricardo Román, chief strategy officer at asset management firm Fracttal, said founders should look beyond taxes and incorporation costs.
“The most important factors are the long-term opportunities a market offers: access to customers, talent, and investment; a predictable regulatory environment; and the ability to scale operations efficiently,” he said to Techli .
Román said Fracttal’s decision to move its operations to Spain was strategic, adding that the company was looking to build on its international presence in the country and expand across Europe.
The move ultimately allowed Fracttal to build on local relationships, better understand the business environment and create a stronger operational presence in the country.
The lessons learned by the startup outside of the Silicon Valley ecosystem apply to other regional startups as well. While having a Bay Area address can be helpful, it does not guarantee customer demand or sound execution. Startups in regional ecosystems may have to build investor relationships more intentionally but also have a great case to make based on access to customers, talent and markets outside of their home city.
Could EU Inc. simplify expansion?
The European Commission adopted its position on a new corporate legal framework to facilitate cross-border business and investment, particularly for startups and scaleups. On October 23, the Council reached its negotiating position for the framework, aiming for online registration within two days at a maximum cost of €100.
The negotiations with the European Parliament are still to come.
Román said that a common framework could help to make the expansion of a company more predictable and reduce the administrative work that currently takes up too much time and resources, which could be better spent on innovation, hiring people and supporting customers.
However, the executive also stressed that legal simplification would not be able to replace the local market knowledge, teams and business relationships.
For founders raising a Series A, there is more than just money on the line; investors are looking for proof that a company can deliver on customer demand and grow as a repeatable business. They are looking for a company with a sound plan for after Series A.

Gasgoo Munich- Gasgoo Embodied Intelligence has learned that Fortsense has officially closed a Series C4 funding round exceeding 400 million yuan. The fresh capital will primarily fund the technical iteration and commercial rollout of its physical AI spatial perception chips.

As autonomous driving shifts from "passive perception" to "active understanding," spatial perception is emerging as a critical layer of infrastructure for the safe operation of physical AI. Leveraging its in-house SPAD chips and all-solid-state optical scanning technology, Fortsense is developing a single-chip RGBD solution. The architecture natively fuses color imagery with depth data on a single chip, fundamentally eliminating the latency and calibration errors typical of traditional multi-sensor setups that pair cameras with LiDAR.
On the commercialization front, the company's solid-state LiDAR SPAD chips have already entered automotive-grade mass production as original equipment for major automakers, with cumulative shipments surpassing 1 million units. Its integrated RGBD chip is slated for commercialization in 2027, targeting next-generation spatial perception applications across smart vehicles, embodied AI, and industrial intelligence. SINOWISDOM noted that as the physical AI sector accelerates, spatial perception chips are poised to see substantially broader market demand.

Soket AI Raises $4 Mn From Bajaj Finance And Pennant For On-Premise LLMs
Soket AI, a Bengaluru-based frontier AI lab building indigenous large language models under the IndiaAI Mission, has raised nearly $4 million from Bajaj Finance and Pennant Technologies.
Bajaj Finance invested about $2 million through Bajaj Finserv Intelligence, the group’s applied research initiative. Pennant Technologies, a lending software company in which Bajaj Finance holds a stake, put in another $2 million. India Accelerator and Finvolve also invested undisclosed amounts.
What the Money Is For
The round is not a general purpose cheque. It is a strategic investment by a lender that wants models it can run inside its own walls.
Read More: Boba Bhai Raises $18 Mn Series B From Left Lane, BIG Capital And Titan Capital
The Soket AI pitch is that its models can be deployed on an organisation’s own infrastructure, including on-premises environments. Trained and run at lower cost than frontier alternatives.
Read More: Style Union Raises Rs 485 Cr Series E Led By Venturi Partners To Expand Beyond South India
For a non-banking finance company handling millions of customer records, that is the whole argument. Data residency and control are procurement conditions, not preferences.
Why a Lender Wants Its Own Model
Financial services companies are testing AI across lending, customer service, risk assessment and cybersecurity.
Each of those use cases touches sensitive customer data. Raises a question that no API provider answers well: where does the data go, and who controls the infrastructure the model runs on.
“The next phase of AI will be defined by outcomes delivered at sustainable cost,” said Rajeev Jain of Bajaj Finance, adding that efficient reasoning-led models can make advanced AI economically viable for financial services while running securely within its own infrastructure.
Sanjiv Bajaj, chairman and managing director of Bajaj Finserv, said the margin for error must be minimal as AI becomes part of critical information infrastructure. Framed the investment as backing indigenous research.
The IndiaAI Mission Angle
Soket AI, a Bengaluru lab, is one of the startups building models under the government’s IndiaAI Mission. Subsidises compute and supports domestic foundation models.
For Soket AI, that backing gives a young lab access to GPU capacity it could not otherwise afford. It gives government buyers a reason to consider the model seriously.
It also creates an expectation. A mission-backed lab is expected to publish benchmarks and demonstrate that its models handle Indian languages and Indian data, not just English benchmarks.
The Competitive Problem
For Soket AI, every Indian enterprise evaluating a domestic model compares it with a global one that is usually better on general reasoning.
For Soket AI, the domestic pitch has to be narrower and more concrete: cheaper inference, control over where data sits. Support that answers within a day.
Soket AI’s claim of efficient reasoning-led models is aimed exactly at that gap, since inference cost is what makes a model viable at scale inside a bank.
The cost argument is the one that survives scrutiny. A bank runs a model on millions of documents a year, so a small difference in cost per token becomes a budget line.
On-premise deployment cuts the API bill but adds hardware and engineering costs. Is why the vendor has to prove the total is still lower.
What to Watch
Three things will show whether Soket AI’s strategy works. The first is a production deployment at Bajaj Finance. A strategic investment that stays a pilot is a research grant.
The second is published evaluation on Indian-language and financial tasks. Is the only way to compare the model honestly with global options.
The third is whether other lenders follow. One group using its own model is a pilot; five would make on-premise AI a standard procurement line.

Oliver Wyman, Marsh’s management consulting business, has agreed to acquire Synpulse, a technology consulting and AI platform company serving banks, insurers, wealth managers and other financial services organizations.
The post Oliver Wyman To Acquire Synpulse To Expand Financial Services Technology And AI Capabilities appeared first on Pulse 2.0 .
candidates.text:
Oliver Wyman To Acquire Synpulse To Expand Financial Services Technology And AI Capabilities
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 4:36 PM
Oliver Wyman To Acquire Synpulse To Expand Financial Services Technology And AI Capabilities
Oliver Wyman, Marsh’s management consulting business, has agreed to acquire Synpulse, a technology consulting and AI platform company serving banks, insurers, wealth managers and other financial services organizations.
The transaction is expected to close in early 2027, subject to customary closing conditions and regulatory approvals. Financial terms were not disclosed.
The acquisition will bring together Oliver Wyman’s strategy consulting capabilities and Synpulse’s technology implementation and AI engineering expertise. The businesses have already worked together through combined teams on multiple client transformation projects.
Financial institutions are adapting to advances in technology, data and AI alongside changing business models. The combination is intended to help clients manage projects across that transition, connecting strategic planning with technology implementation and execution.
Founded in 1996, Synpulse helps financial institutions modernize legacy systems, improve operations and respond to changing customer needs. Its work includes responsible AI strategy and digital ecosystem transformation, supporting clients as they introduce products, simplify processes and develop more personalized customer experiences.
Following the acquisition, Synpulse’s approximately 1,200 employees will continue operating from offices across North America, Europe and Asia.
For Oliver Wyman, the transaction adds technology consulting and engineering resources focused on financial services. For Synpulse, the combination provides greater scale to support clients throughout their digital and AI transformation programs.
The companies also see opportunities to expand across markets, pursue larger and more complex transformation assignments, and strengthen investment in AI and technology capabilities.
Their existing collaboration provides a foundation for the combination, with teams already delivering projects that span strategy and implementation. The acquisition would formalize that relationship and broaden the capabilities available to their financial services clients.
KEY QUOTES
“Our clients don’t separate strategy from technology and execution—they need great ideas to deliver real change. Synpulse brings exceptional technology consulting and AI engineering capabilities, deep financial services expertise and a track record of delivering complex enterprise change. Together, we will deliver a winning combination of talent and technology to help clients achieve their biggest ambitions.”
Ted Moynihan, President And CEO Of Oliver Wyman And Marsh Management Consulting
“Since our founding in 1996, Synpulse has built a strong position as a trusted partner to financial institutions in their digital transformations. Working alongside Oliver Wyman will enable us to support our clients across the entire digital and AI transformation journey, from strategy through implementation and execution. It gives us greater scale to deepen the value we bring to our clients.”
Konrad Niggli, Co-CEO Of Synpulse
“Bringing our teams together creates opportunities to expand our reach across markets, take on larger and more complex transformation projects, and accelerate our growth across regions. It also strengthens our ability to invest in AI and technology, further enhancing the capabilities we bring to our clients.”
Yves Roesti, Co-CEO Of Synpulse
